title: Poppy and seed head in cross-stitch
subtitle: A red field poppy with an ink-blue seed head on 14-count Aida
excerpt: A poppy and seed head is a 50-by-90 stitch piece on 14-count Aida. The scarlet petals, dark eye, and blue-green seed head use six floss colours. The tall vertical composition fits a 10 cm or 15 cm hoop and is worked entirely in full crosses with a back-stitch stem line.
sourceNotes: Original design for Homemade cross-stitch library. Poppy motifs appear throughout British embroidery and natural history illustration traditions.

content.text: A poppy and seed head is a 50-by-90 stitch piece on 14-count
colours cover the scarlet petals with a dark eye, the grey-green stem and leaves, and the blue-green seed head. It is all full crosses except a
line on the stem. The tall composition, about 9 x 16 cm, suits a narrow hoop or a small frame.

items.name: 14-count Aida, cream or white
items.substitutions: Pale linen Aida works well for botanical pieces

items.name: Round hoop or frame
items.qty: 15 cm (6 inch) hoop or narrow frame

content.text: Find the fabric centre. The chart centre falls on the dark eye of the poppy flower. Begin with the eye (310) to anchor the design, then fill the scarlet petals outward (350, 817).
Work the seed head above the stem in 3813 for the main capsule and 523 for the raised ribs. The seed head is a small oval about 10 stitches wide.
Stitch the stem and leaf shapes in the two greens (523 for light areas, 520 for shadow on the underside of leaf shapes).

Add the back-stitch stem line in a single strand of 520, running the length of the stem where the full-cross area is too narrow to fill solidly. A single back-stitch line looks cleaner than a one-stitch-wide column of full crosses.
Wash gently and press face-down until the stitches sit smooth and flat. A slim gold or dark wood frame with no mount makes the most of the vertical composition.

items.symptom: The petal edges look hard and geometric
items.cause: The petal outline was stitched as straight rows without following the curved edge on the chart.
items.fix: Petal curves use single-stitch stepping. Work the outline stitches first to define the shape, then fill inward. Once the outline is complete, fill stitches should sit smooth within the stepped boundary.

items.symptom: The seed head centre looks too light
items.cause: The deep olive green (3011) was not stitched densely enough in the centre.
items.fix: The centre should be fully covered: count the chart squares and make sure every one in the seed head has a cross. Once the fill is complete, the seed head should read as a dark oval that contrasts with the surrounding pod.

content.text: Three botanical stems make a good wall group. Stitch the poppy, daffodil, and tulip separately and frame each in an identical slim frame.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads. The default for beginners. Counted in squares per inch: 11ct, 14ct, 16ct, and 18ct are the common counts.

The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch. Each skein is made of six strands twisted together loosely; the stitcher strips out the number of strands needed for the fabric count (two strands for 14-count Aida) and threads them together.

A solid outline stitch worked in a single strand along the back-stitch layer of the chart. You stitch backwards along the line one stitch at a time, each stitch finishing where the previous one started.
